facts.text: The only hitter of the 1990s to collect 180 hits and score 65 runs or fewer: Garret Anderson, 1998 — 183 H, 62 R.
The only pitcher of the 1990s to walk 130+ batters was Randy Johnson — and he did it twice (1991: 152 BB; 1992: 144 BB).
The only pitcher of the 1990s to allow 35+ homers and still win 15: Pedro Astacio, 1999 — 38 HR allowed, 17-11.
The only pitcher of the 1990s to win 15+ games at age 38 or older: Dennis Martinez, 1993 — 15-9 at 38.
Only two hitters of the 1990s got 200 hits and 100 walks: John Olerud (1993: 200 H, 114 BB); Bernie Williams (1999: 202 H, 100 BB).
The only pitcher of the 1990s to win 25 games: Bob Welch, 1990 — 27-6.
The only hitter of the 1990s to bat .330 at age 22 or younger (500+ PA): Alex Rodriguez, 1996 — .358 at 20.
Only two hitters of the 1990s went 40-40: Alex Rodriguez (1998: 42 HR, 46 SB); Barry Bonds (1996: 42 HR, 40 SB).
Only two hitters of the 1990s hit 30+ homers at age 37 or older: Andres Galarraga (1998: 44 HR at 37); Chili Davis (1997: 30 HR at 37).
The only hitter of the 1990s to bat .310 while slugging under .380 (500+ PA): Willie Randolph, 1991 — .327 AVG, .374 SLG.
Only two hitters of the 1990s drove in 100 runs with an OPS under .700: Joe Carter (2×, best 1990: 115 RBI, .681 OPS); Ruben Sierra (1993: 101 RBI, .678 OPS).
Just three hitters of the 1990s played a full season without a single home run (600+ PA): Otis Nixon (1995: 0 HR in 656 PA); Luis Polonia (1992: 0 HR in 635 PA); Lance Johnson (1991: 0 HR in 624 PA).
Just three pitchers of the 1990s struck out 300 without winning 20: Randy Johnson (3×, best 1999: 364 K, 17-9); Curt Schilling (2×, best 1997: 319 K, 17-11); Pedro Martínez (1997: 305 K, 17-8).
Barry Bonds hit 30+ home runs in 8 straight seasons (1992-99), the longest run of the 1990s.
Frank Thomas drove in 100+ runs in 8 straight seasons (1991-98), the longest run of the 1990s.
Otis Nixon stole 40+ bases in 8 straight seasons (1990-97), the longest run of the 1990s.
Frank Thomas drew 100+ walks in 8 straight seasons (1991-98), the longest run of the 1990s.
Frank Thomas batted .300 or better (500+ PA) in 7 straight seasons (1991-97), the longest run of the 1990s.
Only two pitchers of the 1990s won 12+ games without a start: Mitch Williams (1991: 12-5, 0 GS); Scott Williamson (1999: 12-7, 0 GS).
Only two pitchers of the 1990s posted an ERA under 3.00 and won 7 or fewer (162+ IP): Jose DeLeon (1991: 2.71 ERA, 5-9); Jim Abbott (1992: 2.77 ERA, 7-15).
Only two pitchers of the 1990s won 18+ games at age 22 or younger: Ramon Martinez (1990: 20-6 at 22); Steve Avery (1991: 18-8 at 21).
Lee Smith saved 30+ games in 6 straight seasons (1990-95), the longest run of the 1990s.
Just three hitters of the 1990s hit 45 doubles and 5 homers or fewer: Mark Grudzielanek (1997: 54 2B, 4 HR); Jody Reed (1990: 45 2B, 5 HR); Chuck Knoblauch (1994: 45 2B, 5 HR).
Randy Johnson struck out 200+ in 5 straight seasons (1991-95), the longest run of the 1990s.
Just three hitters of the 1990s grounded into 28+ double plays: Ivan Rodriguez (1999: 31 GIDP); George Bell (1992: 29 GIDP); Cal Ripken Jr. (1996: 28 GIDP).
Just three hitters of the 1990s hit 35+ homers with 15 doubles or fewer: Mark McGwire (1995: 39 HR, 13 2B); David Justice (1993: 40 HR, 15 2B); José Canseco (1990: 37 HR, 14 2B).

Just three hitters of the 1990s stole 40+ bases with an on-base under .300 (400+ PA): Vince Coleman (1994: 50 SB, .285 OBP); Delino DeShields (1996: 48 SB, .288 OBP); Brian L. Hunter (2×, best 1999: 44 SB, .280 OBP).
Just three hitters of the 1990s hit 30+ homers at age 22 or younger: Juan Gonzalez (1992: 43 HR at 22); Alex Rodriguez (2×, best 1998: 42 HR at 22); Andruw Jones (1998: 31 HR at 21).
Just three hitters of the 1990s stole 30+ bases while getting caught 3 times or fewer: Brady Anderson (1994: 31 SB, 1 CS); Doug Glanville (1999: 34 SB, 2 CS); Roberto Alomar (1995: 30 SB, 3 CS).

Just three hitters of the 1990s struck out 30 times or fewer in a full season (600+ PA): Ozzie Smith (1993: 18 K in 603 PA); Tony Gwynn (2×, best 1990: 23 K in 629 PA); Gregg Jefferies (1992: 29 K in 657 PA).

Just four hitters of the 1990s batted .320 or better with 25 walks or fewer (500+ PA): Andres Galarraga (1993: .370, 24 BB); Dante Bichette (1995: .340, 22 BB); Homer Bush (1999: .320, 21 BB); Ivan Rodriguez (1999: .332, 24 BB).

Just four pitchers of the 1990s posted an ERA under 2.00 (162+ IP): Greg Maddux (2×, best 1994: 1.56 ERA in 202.0 IP); Kevin Brown (1996: 1.89 ERA in 233.0 IP); Pedro Martínez (1997: 1.90 ERA in 241.1 IP); Roger Clemens (1990: 1.93 ERA in 228.1 IP).
5 hitters drove in 150 runs in the 1990s. The most extreme: Manny Ramirez, 1999 — 165 RBI.
9 pitchers saved 35 games and struck out 100 in the 1990s (10 seasons). The most extreme: Billy Wagner, 1999 — 39 SV, 124 K in 74.2 IP.
Lowest average by any 100-RBI hitter of the 1990s: Joe Carter, 1990 — .232 with 115 RBI.
Most strikeouts by a .300 hitter of the 1990s: Sammy Sosa, 1998 — 171 K while batting .308.
Most steals by a 30-homer hitter of the 1990s: Barry Bonds, 1990 — 52 SB with 33 HR.
Most home runs per RBI of the 1990s: Rob Deer, 1992 — 32 HR but only 64 RBI.
Fewest strikeouts by a 30-homer hitter of the 1990s: Gary Sheffield, 1992 — 40 K with 33 HR.
Highest average by a hitter with 3 homers or fewer: Willie Randolph, 1991 — .327 with 0 HR.
Most walks by a sub-.240 hitter of the 1990s: Mickey Tettleton, 1992 — 122 BB while batting .238.
Most RBI per home run among 100-RBI seasons: Paul Molitor, 1996 — 113 RBI on 9 HR.
Most wins by a pitcher with an ERA over 5.00: Kevin Ritz, 1996 — 17-11 with a 5.28 ERA.
Fewest wins by a qualified pitcher with an ERA under 3.00: Jose DeLeon, 1991 — 5-9 despite a 2.71 ERA.
Most strikeouts by a pitcher with a losing record: Roger Clemens, 1996 — 257 K, 10-13.
Most losses by a pitcher with an ERA under 3.50: Greg Swindell, 1991 — 9-16 with a 3.48 ERA.
Fewest strikeouts by a 20-game winner of the 1990s: Bill Gullickson, 1991 — 91 K, 20-9.
Most innings in a season without a complete game: Ismael Valdez, 1996 — 225.0 IP, 0 CG.
Most home runs allowed in a season this decade: Rick Helling, 1999 — 41 HR allowed, 13-11.
Most walks by a 15-game winner: Russ Ortiz, 1999 — 125 BB, 18-9.
10 hitter-seasons of the 1990s ended on exactly 99 RBI, one short of 100 — among them Todd Zeile (1996), Raúl Mondesi (1999), Sean Casey (1999).
10 teams of the 1990s won 100 games; the best record was the 1998 Yankees at 114-48.
Oldest player of the 1990s to hit 30 home runs: Chili Davis, age 37 in 1997 — 30 HR.
Oldest player of the 1990s to bat .330 (500+ PA): Paul Molitor, age 39 in 1996 — .341.
Oldest player of the 1990s to drive in 100 runs: Dave Winfield, age 40 in 1992 — 108 RBI.
Youngest player of the 1990s to steal 40 bases: Delino DeShields, age 21 in 1990 — 42 SB.
Oldest player of the 1990s to steal 40 bases: Rickey Henderson, age 39 in 1998 — 66 SB.
Youngest player of the 1990s to win 20 games: Ramon Martinez, age 22 in 1990 — 20-6.
Oldest player of the 1990s to win 20 games: Jack Morris, age 37 in 1992 — 21-6.
Youngest player of the 1990s to strike out 200: Kerry Wood, age 21 in 1998 — 233 K.
Oldest player of the 1990s to strike out 200: Nolan Ryan Jr., age 44 in 1991 — 203 K.
Youngest player of the 1990s to post a qualified ERA under 2.75: Mike Mussina, age 23 in 1992 — 2.54 ERA.
Oldest player of the 1990s to post a qualified ERA under 2.75: Dennis Martinez, age 37 in 1992 — 2.47 ERA.
5 pitcher-seasons of the 1990s ended on exactly 39 saves, one short of 40 — among them Jeff Montgomery (1992), Mark Wohlers (1996), Billy Wagner (1999).
4 hitter-seasons of the 1990s ended on a .299 average, one point short of .300 — among them Mark McGwire (1998), Bobby Higginson (1997), Darin Erstad (1997).
4 hitter-seasons of the 1990s ended on exactly 199 hits, one short of 200 — among them Terry Pendleton (1992), Andy Van Slyke (1992), Willie McGee (1990).
8 teams of the 1990s had two players at 40+ home runs; the biggest pairing was the 1997 Colorado Rockies — Larry Walker 49, Andres Galarraga 41, Vinny Castilla 40.
33 teams of the 1990s had three players at 100+ RBI; the biggest pairing was the 1999 Cleveland Indians — Manny Ramirez 165, Roberto Alomar 120, Richie Sexson 116.
4 teams of the 1990s had two players at 200+ hits; the biggest pairing was the 1991 Texas Rangers — Rafael Palmeiro 203, Ruben Sierra 203, Julio Franco 201.
12 teams of the 1990s had two players at 40+ steals; the biggest pairing was the 1990 Montreal Expos — Otis Nixon 50, Tim Raines Sr. 49, Delino DeShields 42.
4 teams of the 1990s had two players at 20 wins; the biggest pairing was the 1990 Oakland Athletics — Bob Welch 27, Dave Stewart 22.
Most home runs of the 1990s: Mark McGwire, 405 across 10 seasons.
Most home runs in the 1990s by a hitter who never led the majors in a season: Ken Griffey Jr., 382.
Most hits of the 1990s: Mark Grace, 1754.
Most strikeouts by a hitter in the 1990s: Sammy Sosa, 1322.
Most triples of the 1990s: Lance Johnson, 113.
Most RBI of the 1990s: Albert Belle, 1099.
Most wins of the 1990s: Greg Maddux, 176.
Most losses of the 1990s: Andy Benes, 116 — and 125 wins.
Most complete games of the 1990s: Greg Maddux, 75.
Most saves of the 1990s: John Wetteland, 295.
1999 had 45 30-homer hitters, the most of any season in the 1990s.
1992 had just 10 30-homer hitters, the fewest of any season in the 1990s.
1999 had 55 .300 hitters (500+ PA), the most of any season in the 1990s.
1994 had just 6 .300 hitters (500+ PA), the fewest of any season in the 1990s.
1999 had 59 100-RBI hitters, the most of any season in the 1990s.
1994 had just 5 100-RBI hitters, the fewest of any season in the 1990s.
1992 had 18 40-steal players, the most of any season in the 1990s.
1994 had just 3 40-steal players, the fewest of any season in the 1990s.
1996 had 8 200-hit seasons, the most of any season in the 1990s.
1990 had no 200-hit seasons at all — one of the seasons of the 1990s without one.
1990 had 6 20-game winners, the most of any season in the 1990s.
1994 had no 20-game winners at all — one of the seasons of the 1990s without one.
1996 had 12 200-strikeout pitchers, the most of any season in the 1990s.
1994 had just 1 200-strikeout pitchers, the fewest of any season in the 1990s.
5 teams of the 1990s lost 100 games; the worst was the 1996 Tigers at 53-109.
Best run differential of the 1990s: the 1998 Yankees, +309 (965 scored, 656 allowed).
6 hitters stole 70 bases in the 1990s (8 seasons). The most extreme: Marquis Grissom, 1992 — 78 SB.
5 hitters batted .320 at age 37 or older (500+ PA) in the 1990s (7 seasons). The most extreme: Tony Gwynn, 1997 — .372 at 37.
2 hitter-seasons of the 1990s ended on exactly 49 steals, one short of 50 — among them Roberto Alomar (1992), Tim Raines Sr. (1990).

method: Every fact is a predicate evaluated over every hitter-season and pitcher-season in the decade, pulled in full from the MLB Stats API (the official record). Nothing is recalled or estimated; the rows that satisfy each rule are stored with it.

'Only', 'two' and 'three/four' claims are exact counts across the complete pull. Where a rule uses a plate-appearance or innings floor instead of a league qualification bar, the floor is stated in the fact so the claim is reproducible.
Thresholds are era-aware (strikeouts, saves and home runs meant different things in 1925 and 1995) and are recorded in the file.
Rules built from plain comparisons carry a Stathead Season Finder spec with the same filters and year range, for independent re-checking on the subscription.
